string.text: {=spc_wc_khusraw_prebackstory}You want to hear where I have been? Very well - pour the tea, and I will tell you, though the tale is a long one.

{=spc_wc_khusraw_backstory_a}I was once a tax official in Khorasan, comfortable enough, until a dream shook me from that life - I sold what I owned, and set out on the road to Mecca with nothing but my staff and my questions.

{=spc_wc_khusraw_backstory_b}Seven years I walked, in disguise more often than not, through Egypt and Syria and the Hijaz, writing down what I saw, what I learned, who I met - a poor man's eyes see a city a rich man never could.

{=spc_wc_khusraw_backstory_c}When I finally turned home, I found that what I had learned in Cairo did not sit well with everyone I met on the road back - some men prefer their questions unasked. So I have kept walking, teaching where I am welcome, writing when I am not.
{=spc_wc_khusraw_response_1}A traveler's education is worth more than any madrasa's, I'd wager.
{=spc_wc_khusraw_response_2}A wandering heretic with too many opinions, more like. Watch your tongue in my camp.

{=spc_wc_khusraw_backstory_d}I can read a road better than most men read a book, and I know when a caravan is being watched. I have also picked up more of medicine than I ever meant to, out of necessity.

{=spc_wc_khusraw_generic_backstory}I spent seven years walking the roads of the Islamic world in disguise, recording everything I saw. I know how to move unseen, and how to talk my way past anyone who might stop me.
{=spc_wc_khayyam_prebackstory}My story? It is mostly numbers and stars, I'm afraid - less exciting than you might hope, but I will tell it.

{=spc_wc_khayyam_backstory_a}The Sultan's own vizier once summoned me to Isfahan to fix the calendar itself - the old reckoning had drifted so far that the seasons no longer matched the months. I built the observatory myself, more or less.

{=spc_wc_khayyam_backstory_b}We measured the length of the year to a precision that will outlast us both, I think - the calendar we made is truer than the one most kingdoms still use. But viziers fall, and patrons die, and observatories are expensive to keep without one.

{=spc_wc_khayyam_backstory_c}So here I am, between patrons, doing what mathematicians have always done when the funding dries up - looking for someone new who wants their numbers, their walls, or their finances put in proper order.
{=spc_wc_khayyam_response_1}A man who can measure the stars can surely manage a campaign's supply lines.
{=spc_wc_khayyam_response_2}Poetry and astronomy won't win you many battles, I'm afraid.
{=spc_wc_khayyam_backstory_d}I can plan a siege's geometry as easily as a horoscope, and I keep better accounts than most stewards you'll find in a tavern.

{=spc_wc_khayyam_generic_backstory}I built the Sultan's observatory and reformed the calendar itself, when I had a patron for it. Numbers, walls, and treasuries all bend to the same logic, if you know how to look.
{=spc_wc_psellos_prebackstory}You wish to know my history? I have advised more emperors than I care to count, and outlasted most of them. Sit, and I will tell you how that is done.
{=spc_wc_psellos_backstory_a}I came up through the Imperial chancery as a young man with a gift for rhetoric and a sharper gift for reading which way the wind was about to turn in the palace.

{=spc_wc_psellos_backstory_b}I have written the history of this court's last several reigns myself, and I assure you, the men who wrote themselves as heroes rarely were. I served whoever sat the throne, and made sure my own name never sat too close to the ones who fell.

{=spc_wc_psellos_backstory_c}The trouble with surviving so many emperors is that eventually the survivors stop trusting you, on principle. So I find myself, for the moment, at leisure - which is to say, unemployed by anyone with a throne.
{=spc_wc_psellos_response_1}A man who can survive that many changes of fortune is exactly who I want advising me.
{=spc_wc_psellos_response_2}A man who has betrayed that many masters is exactly who I do NOT want at my back.
{=spc_wc_psellos_backstory_d}I can talk my way into rooms other men are barred from, and I know more of court intrigue and old grudges than is probably healthy for me to know.

{=spc_wc_psellos_generic_backstory}I have advised a long succession of emperors and written the history of their reigns myself. There is very little in the way of court politics or old scandal that I have not already seen.
{=spc_wc_roussel_prebackstory}My story. Fine. Pour the wine first - it is not a short one, and it does not end well for the men who trusted me.
{=spc_wc_roussel_backstory_a}I led Norman lances for the Emperor's own army, and I was at Manzikert when the whole thing came apart - most men ran, or died. I did neither.

{=spc_wc_roussel_backstory_b}After that disaster I decided the Empire's coin was better spent on my own ambitions than theirs, so I raised my own banner in Anatolia and held a city as my own for a time. Long enough to know what it feels like to be more than just a captain.

{=spc_wc_roussel_backstory_c}It did not last. The Sultan's own Turks were paid to bring me down where the Emperor's men could not, and I was handed over in chains, like a debt finally collected. I bought my way loose of that, eventually. Men with useful swords always do.
{=spc_wc_roussel_response_1}A man who can carve out his own principality once can do it again - under better management.
{=spc_wc_roussel_response_2}A traitor twice over, then. I'll not turn my back on you.
{=spc_wc_roussel_backstory_d}I know how to hold a line of cavalry together when everyone around me is running, and I know how to make men follow me who owe me nothing.

{=spc_wc_roussel_generic_backstory}I commanded Norman mercenaries for the Empire, fought at Manzikert, and later carved out my own short-lived principality in Anatolia before it was taken from me. I know how to lead, and how to survive a rout.
{=spc_wc_ghazali_prebackstory}My story is not one I tell for entertainment, but you have asked honestly, so I will answer honestly.
{=spc_wc_ghazali_backstory_a}I held the finest teaching post in Baghdad, at the Nizamiyya - students came from every corner of the caliphate to hear me. I had wealth, reputation, certainty.

{=spc_wc_ghazali_backstory_b}And then, one year, I found I no longer believed a word I was teaching. Not the substance of it - the point of it. I could argue any position brilliantly and prove nothing to my own soul. So I gave it all up and walked away from Baghdad with nothing.

{=spc_wc_ghazali_backstory_c}I spent years after that with nothing but a robe and my own doubts, sleeping where I could, eating what was given. I found something on that road I never found in the lecture hall. I still do not know if I can put it into words you would find satisfying.
{=spc_wc_ghazali_response_1}A man who questions his own certainty that deeply is a man worth listening to.
{=spc_wc_ghazali_response_2}A man who abandoned wealth and comfort for doubt is a fool, however clever his doubts.
{=spc_wc_ghazali_backstory_d}I can still out-argue any man in your camp, and years on the road taught me more of patience and people than the madrasa ever did.

{=spc_wc_ghazali_generic_backstory}I once taught at Baghdad's finest school, then abandoned it all in a crisis of conscience to wander as an ascetic for years. I have made my peace since - mostly - and I know how to counsel a household as well as debate a scholar.
{=spc_wc_usama_prebackstory}You want stories of the Franks? I have plenty - I have spent half my life among them, one way or another.

{=spc_wc_usama_backstory_a}I was raised in Shaizar to the sword and the pen both - my family expected both of me, and I never saw why I should choose. I have hunted, fought, and written verse in the same year more times than I can count.

{=spc_wc_usama_backstory_b}Living so close to the Frankish lords, I came to know them better than most of our people ever will - some are ignorant brutes, true, but others I have called friend, and shared a table with, oddly enough. It is a strange, complicated business, and anyone who tells you it is simple has never actually lived it.

{=spc_wc_usama_backstory_c}My own family's fortunes have risen and fallen more times than I care to recount, and a man of the pen with no post finds himself, eventually, offering that pen and that sword to whoever will make good use of both.
{=spc_wc_usama_response_1}A man who understands both sides of that war is worth ten who only understand one.
{=spc_wc_usama_response_2}Too friendly with the Franks for my taste, if I'm honest.
{=spc_wc_usama_backstory_d}I can hunt, ride, and fight as well as any warrior you'll find, and I have dealt with more courts and more Frankish lords than most men in this camp have ever laid eyes on.

{=spc_wc_usama_generic_backstory}I was raised as both warrior and poet in Shaizar, and I have spent much of my life dealing directly with the Frankish lords of the coast - a rare and complicated education.
{=spc_wc_petritsi_prebackstory}You wish to know my history? It begins, as these things often do, in a library far from here.

{=spc_wc_petritsi_backstory_a}I studied in Constantinople, at the Mangana - Greek philosophy, the old pagan thinkers our own priests are often suspicious of. I brought that learning home to Georgia hoping to build something with it.

{=spc_wc_petritsi_backstory_b}Not everyone in our own church welcomed what I brought back. Translating a pagan philosopher into our tongue is, to some clerics, one step removed from heresy, whatever the King's own academy thinks of the matter. I have had my defenders and my enemies in equal measure.
{=spc_wc_petritsi_backstory_c}For now, between patrons and away from the schools, I find myself on the road, which at least gives a philosopher time to think - if rather less time to write.
{=spc_wc_petritsi_response_1}A scholar who can navigate both a royal court and its clergy is no small asset.
{=spc_wc_petritsi_response_2}A dabbler in pagan philosophy - I'd rather my household stayed simple and pious.
{=spc_wc_petritsi_backstory_d}I have a physician's training as well as a philosopher's mind, and I can manage a household's accounts as easily as I once managed an academy's.

{=spc_wc_petritsi_generic_backstory}I studied Greek philosophy in Constantinople and brought it home to Georgia, translating the old pagan thinkers for a new audience - not without controversy. I know how to run a household and tend to the sick besides.
{=spc_wc_vardan_prebackstory}My story? Ask around Svaneti first - they'll have a version before I've even opened my mouth. But I'll give you mine.
{=spc_wc_vardan_backstory_a}I was eristavi of Svaneti, a duke in my own right in the high valleys, until a new King took the throne who I did not trust to respect what was ours.

{=spc_wc_vardan_backstory_b}So I raised the Svans and rose against him. It seemed the right thing to do at the time - our valleys have always governed themselves, and I did not care to see that end because a young king wanted to prove himself. It did not go the way I hoped.

{=spc_wc_vardan_backstory_c}The revolt was put down, my title is not what it once was, and my welcome in the lowlands is thin at best. A duke without a duchy is just a man with a sword and old grudges, so that is what I have become.
{=spc_wc_vardan_response_1}A man who'll rise against a king he doesn't trust is a man of principle, whatever the cost.
{=spc_wc_vardan_response_2}A man who leads his own people into a lost cause is a man I don't need leading anyone in my company.
{=spc_wc_vardan_backstory_d}I know the high passes better than any lowlander ever will, and I can still put an arrow or a spear where I mean to.
{=spc_wc_vardan_generic_backstory}I was a highland duke in Svaneti who rose against the King and lost. I know the mountains, I know how to fight, and I have no love left for the men who beat me.
{=spc_wc_peterhermit_prebackstory}Ah - you want to hear how I came to be walking these roads instead of leading an army east? Sit, friend, it is a hard story to tell.

{=spc_wc_peterhermit_backstory_a}I preached the taking up of the cross before any lord had raised his banner for it - thousands followed me east, common folk mostly, farmers and their families, believing God himself would clear our path.

{=spc_wc_peterhermit_backstory_b}God did not clear our path. The Turks met us before we ever reached the Holy Land, and what had followed me out of Europe with such faith was broken apart in a single terrible day near Nicaea. I have not stopped hearing it since.

{=spc_wc_peterhermit_backstory_c}I survived - I am ashamed some days that I survived - and made my way after the lords' own army that came after us, better armed and better led than I ever managed to be. I still believe in the cause. I no longer trust myself to lead it.
{=spc_wc_peterhermit_response_1}Faith that strong, even after a disaster like that, is worth more than any sword.
{=spc_wc_peterhermit_response_2}A preacher who led thousands to their deaths through his own naivete - I want no part of that.

{=spc_wc_peterhermit_backstory_d}I can still move a crowd or a camp with nothing but words, and there are few men left who understand what it truly costs to lead the faithful astray, even with the best of intentions.

{=spc_wc_peterhermit_generic_backstory}I led the common folk east ahead of the great lords' armies, and watched most of them die near Nicaea for it. I still believe in the cause - I have simply learned, at terrible cost, what faith alone cannot do.
{=spc_wc_bartholomew_prebackstory}You want to hear about the Lance? Everyone does, sooner or later. Sit down - I'll tell you exactly what I saw, and you can decide for yourself what to believe.

{=spc_wc_bartholomew_backstory_a}I was a pilgrim, nobody of any importance, starving along with the rest of the army inside the walls of Antioch, when I began to have visions - Saint Andrew, telling me where the Holy Lance itself lay buried, beneath the very cathedral we were trapped in.

{=spc_wc_bartholomew_backstory_b}I led the digging myself, and by God, we found a lance - I held it up before an army that had nothing left but despair, and something changed in every man who saw it. We broke the siege the very next day. You cannot argue with that, whatever else you believe.

{=spc_wc_bartholomew_backstory_c}Not everyone believed me, before or after. Some of the great lords thought it a starving man's fever-dream, or worse, a fraud staged for morale. I proved myself in the fire, in the end, whatever it cost me. I do not care to speak further of that day.
{=spc_wc_bartholomew_response_1}Whatever the truth of the vision, you broke that siege. That's proof enough for me.
{=spc_wc_bartholomew_response_2}A convenient vision from a man with nothing to lose, and a very suspicious trial afterward. I have my doubts.
{=spc_wc_bartholomew_backstory_d}I can move an army with a story better than most men can move it with a whip, and I have walked through fire, quite literally, for what I believe in.

{=spc_wc_bartholomew_generic_backstory}I found the Holy Lance at Antioch when the army had nothing left but despair, and I proved my claim in a trial by fire few men would dare attempt. Believe what you like about the vision - the siege broke the very next day.

{=spc_wc_matthew_prebackstory}You want history? I have been writing it down as it happens, all around me - Byzantines, Turks, Armenians, and now you Franks besides. Sit, and I'll tell you a piece of it.

{=spc_wc_matthew_backstory_a}I took to the monastery young, in Edessa, in a country that has changed hands more times in my own life than I care to count - Byzantine governors, then Turkish raids, then Frankish counts, one after another.

{=spc_wc_matthew_backstory_b}I began keeping a record of it all, because someone had to, and because I did not trust any single court's version of events to survive when that court inevitably fell. History written only by the victors is not history at all, in my view.

{=spc_wc_matthew_backstory_c}Edessa is a Frankish county now, and I keep writing, though my sympathies and my safety do not always sit in the same place. A chronicler learns to be careful about which page he shows to which lord.
{=spc_wc_matthew_response_1}A man who writes the truth regardless of who's currently in power - that takes real courage.
{=spc_wc_matthew_response_2}A scribbler with opinions about every faction is a man who trusts no one - including you.
{=spc_wc_matthew_backstory_d}I know the history and grievances of every people in this land better than most lords know their own family trees, and that knowledge has its uses.

{=spc_wc_matthew_generic_backstory}I have chronicled this region through Byzantine, Turkish, and now Frankish rule from my monastery in Edessa. Few men alive understand this land's tangled politics as well as I do, for better or worse.
{=spc_wc_heratsi_prebackstory}You want to know my trade? Simple enough - I keep men from dying who would otherwise die. The rest is just study.

{=spc_wc_heratsi_backstory_a}I trained in the old way, the way that draws from the Persians, the Arabs, and the Greeks all together - Cilicia sits at the crossing of all three traditions, and a good physician here learns to take what works from each.

{=spc_wc_heratsi_backstory_b}I have written down what I know of fevers, because too many good men die of causes a trained hand could have caught in time, and too much of that knowledge dies with the physician who never wrote it anywhere.

{=spc_wc_heratsi_backstory_c}Physicians who write their knowledge down instead of guarding it as a secret do not always make friends among the guild, but I would rather my knowledge outlive me than die with me. So here I am, still practicing, still writing, and still looking for a household worth serving.
{=spc_wc_heratsi_response_1}A physician who shares his knowledge freely is exactly the kind of man I want tending my camp.
{=spc_wc_heratsi_response_2}Physicians who write everything down for anyone to read rarely have anything worth stealing in the first place.
{=spc_wc_heratsi_backstory_d}I can treat wounds and fevers better than any camp healer you have met, and I keep meticulous notes on every patient, which has saved more lives than luck ever has.

{=spc_wc_heratsi_generic_backstory}I trained in the Perso-Arabo-Greek medical tradition here in Cilicia and have written down my knowledge of fevers rather than keep it secret. I can keep your men alive through wounds that would otherwise finish them.
{=spc_wc_kashgari_prebackstory}You wish to know where I've been? Further than most men in this tavern have ever dreamed of walking, and I wrote down every word I heard along the way.

{=spc_wc_kashgari_backstory_a}I was born to a prominent family near Kashgar, but I gave up whatever comfortable path was laid out for me to travel instead among every Turkic people I could find - Oghuz, Kipchak, Karluk, and more besides.

{=spc_wc_kashgari_backstory_b}I collected their words, their proverbs, their poetry, their names for the stars and the seasons - a great dictionary of every Turkic tongue, because I saw that each tribe thought its own dialect the only proper one, and I wanted to prove that we were, all of us, part of the same great family of peoples.

{=spc_wc_kashgari_backstory_c}I presented the finished work to the Caliph's own court in Baghdad, hoping it might serve to bind Turk and Arab a little closer together. Whether it did what I hoped, I cannot say. But the work exists, and it is mine, and no one can take that from me now.
{=spc_wc_kashgari_response_1}A man who spent his life proving all the Turkic peoples are one family - that's a rare kind of wisdom.
{=spc_wc_kashgari_response_2}A dictionary won't win you any battles. I need swords, not scholars.
{=spc_wc_kashgari_backstory_d}I have walked further across the steppe and the settled lands both than most scouts you'll ever hire, and I speak more dialects than I can easily count.

{=spc_wc_kashgari_generic_backstory}I traveled across every Turkic-speaking land I could reach and compiled the first great dictionary of our tongues and traditions. Few men know the steppe, its peoples, and its many roads as well as I do.
{=spc_wc_yasawi_prebackstory}You want to know my path? It began with loss, if I am honest with you, and it has not been a simple one since.

{=spc_wc_yasawi_backstory_a}I lost my father young, and was raised instead by another teacher, a Sufi master who took me in and taught me what the scholars of the cities never bothered teaching to steppe-born boys like myself.

{=spc_wc_yasawi_backstory_b}I have spent my years since trying to carry that teaching to people the great mosques and madrasas of the cities never much cared to reach - herders, wanderers, common folk who wanted God brought to them in their own tongue, in verse they could actually understand and sing.

{=spc_wc_yasawi_backstory_c}Some of the learned men in the cities look down on that kind of teaching, plain verse for plain people instead of Arabic argument for scholars. I have made my peace with their disapproval. The people I have actually taught seem to have found something real in it, and that matters more to me than a scholar's approval.
{=spc_wc_yasawi_response_1}Bringing faith to common folk in words they understand - that's a rare and generous gift.
{=spc_wc_yasawi_response_2}Simple verse for simple people. I prefer men who can debate the finer points, myself.

{=spc_wc_yasawi_backstory_d}I can speak to any common soldier in your camp in words that actually reach them, and I have more patience for the frightened and the grieving than most men ever bother to have.

{=spc_wc_yasawi_generic_backstory}I was raised by a Sufi master after losing my own father young, and have spent my life bringing faith to common people in plain verse rather than scholarly argument. I know how to speak to soldiers and villagers alike, in words that actually reach them.
